what: NewMarket makes chemical additives for fuels and lubricants. Through its Afton Chemical business it sells the additive packages that engine oil, transmission fluid and fuel blenders mix into their products to prevent wear, control deposits and extend oil life.
customers: Oil majors and lubricant blenders worldwide, plus fuel refiners and marketers. Additive packages are formulated for a customer's specific product and qualified against industry specifications.
money: Lubricant and fuel additive packages sold to oil companies and blenders globally.
Tetraethyl lead for remaining legacy uses, and other specialty chemistry.
moat: Additive formulations have to pass expensive industry engine tests, and once a lubricant blender's product is approved with a particular additive package, changing supplier means repeating that testing. Only a handful of companies worldwide can do this work, which keeps the industry structurally concentrated and pricing rational.
risks: Revenue has been flat at about $2.7B to $2.8B for four years, so growth comes from margin and buybacks rather than volume.
The long-term shift to electric vehicles reduces demand for engine oil additives, which is the largest end use.
Base chemical and oil feedstock costs move margins between quarters until price increases catch up.
No analysts are shown as covering the stock, so there is no external consensus to compare against.
Debt of $961.6M against only $77.6M of cash means the company depends on steady cash generation to service it.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 14.5 times earnings and 10.8 times EV/EBITDA for a business with very high barriers to entry.
Free cash flow of $383.4M on $2.8B of revenue funds a long record of share repurchases, which has steadily reduced the share count.
Heavy-duty trucking, marine and industrial lubricants are much slower to electrify than passenger cars, and they use more additive per litre.
Growth in vehicle fleets in developing markets continues to raise global lubricant volumes.
watch: Volume growth in heavy-duty and industrial additives. Passenger car oil will decline over decades; whether the heavy-duty and industrial side grows fast enough to offset it determines the long-run value.
